rationale: The printed entry defines the great fish/sea-monster as 'a devouring kingdom that swallows and is forced to give back,' and the two texts printed with the entry state that identification almost verbatim: Jeremiah 51:34 has Babylon's king 'swallowed me up like a dragon, he hath filled his belly... he hath cast me out,' and Jeremiah 51:44 (quoted in the chapter) has God 'bring forth out of his mouth that which he hath swallowed'; Ezekiel 32:2 explicitly calls Pharaoh 'a whale in the seas,' with Ezekiel 29:3 calling him 'the great dragon.' No comparable text ever calls a fish or its belly the grave. The strongest rival reading — the fish's belly as the grave/Sheol, a providential instrument prefiguring the tomb — cannot account for these prophetic texts, where the swallowing monster is unambiguously an empire and the swallow-hold-disgorge itinerary matches Jonah's exactly. The book's kingdom reading, by contrast, absorbs the counter's evidence: Jonah's 'belly of Sheol' language and the Matthean typology are explained as the death-like captivity inside a devouring power that is compelled to release its prey (resurrection). The recognized common alternative that sea-monsters figure hostile empires (Egypt, Babylon) actually agrees with the book's core, showing the book is a sharpened form of an already-standard identification rather than an isolated novelty. Secondary elaborations (Jerusalem as 'the heart of the earth,' the day-count, day-as-thousand-years) remain contestable but are not needed for the core.
book_core_identification: The 'great fish' / sea-monster (dag gadol, kētos, tannin, dragon, whale) symbolizes a devouring kingdom/empire: a great body of men moving through the sea of the nations as one, which swallows its victims alive, holds them in its belly, and is divinely compelled to give them back.
book_secondary_elaborations: The specific application that Jerusalem (spiritually Egypt, Rev 11:8) riding Rome is the kingdom that swallowed the Messiah
'The heart of the earth' (Matt 12:40) identified as Jerusalem rather than the tomb, dissolving the three-days counting problem
The scaling principle: one fish = one man in the sea of nations; a great fish = a kingdom

The scene-by-scene mapping of Jonah's whole book onto the Passion narrative (fare/silver, sleeper, lots, innocent blood, reeds/crown, gentile worshippers, Nineveh as post-resurrection gentile mission)
The suph/reeds wordplay linking Jonah's weeds to the Red Sea crossing
The three-days'-journey city read via the day-as-thousand-years scale
Jonah's anger as prophecy of Israel's jealousy at gentile inclusion (Rom 11:11)
strongest_counter_interpretation: The mainstream reading: Jonah's great fish is a divinely appointed instrument of providence whose belly symbolizes the grave/Sheol — the realm of death from which God delivers — functioning typologically as the tomb of Christ per Jesus' own 'sign of Jonah' saying (Matt 12:39-40); it is not a political kingdom. Separately, sea-monster texts (Leviathan, Rahab, tannin) carry chaos-combat imagery of God-opposing powers, kept distinct from Jonah's fish.
counter_core_identification: The great fish's belly = the grave/Sheol/realm of death; the fish itself is a providential instrument of judgment and deliverance prefiguring burial and resurrection, with no imperial or political referent.
material_core_denial: The counter denies that the fish is a kingdom at all: it holds that the fish symbolizes death/the grave (or is merely a providential creature), so the same referent cannot be both a literal-providential death-symbol and a corporate political empire in the entry's sense.
counter_case: Jonah himself locates his confinement in death terms: 'out of the belly of hell [Sheol] cried I' (Jonah 2:2), 'the earth with her bars was about me for ever' (Jonah 2:6)
Jesus' own application compares the fish's belly to 'the heart of the earth' — read by nearly all interpreters as the tomb (Matt 12:40)
Jonah 1:17 says the LORD 'prepared' the fish, presenting it as a providential creature in a narrative, not an allegorical polity
The chaoskampf texts (Job 41; Ps 74:13-14; Isa 27:1; 51:9-10) are a distinct symbolic stream about primordial/cosmic powers and should not be imported into Jonah
Standard scholarship keeps ordinary fish, Jonah's fish, and mythic sea-monsters as separate figures rather than one uniform symbol
book_explanatory_advantages: Jeremiah 51:34 is scripture's own explicit key: a kingdom (Babylon) 'swallowed me up like a dragon... filled his belly... cast me out' — precisely Jonah's swallow-hold-disgorge itinerary applied to an empire and its captives
Ezekiel 32:2 and 29:3 explicitly name a king/kingdom (Pharaoh/Egypt) as 'a whale in the seas' and 'the great dragon' — a direct scriptural equation of sea-monster with kingdom

Jeremiah 51:44 supplies the 'forced to give back' clause verbatim: 'I will bring forth out of his mouth that which he hath swallowed up' — explaining why the fish must vomit Jonah out and why the tomb could not hold Christ (Acts 2:24)

The reading coheres with the book's established symbol-system: sea = peoples/nations (Rev 17:15), mountains = kingdoms (Rev 17:9-10), making 'great fish in the sea' = great body of men among the nations a consistent scaling rather than an ad hoc claim
It explains why Jonah is alive and praying inside the fish (Jonah 2:1) — captivity within a devouring power, not literal death — which the grave reading must treat loosely

It explains the Babylon/Jonah contrast the chapter draws: Babylon cast into the sea 'shall not rise' (Jer 51:64) while Jonah cast into the same sea rises, matching the baptism typology (Rom 6:4; Mic 7:19)
Even the common interpretation's own alternative concedes sea-monsters figure 'hostile empires such as Egypt and Babylon' from the very texts printed with the entry
counter_explanatory_advantages: It preserves the plain narrative register of Jonah 1:17 (an appointed creature) without an added symbolic layer
Jonah's own 'belly of Sheol' prayer language gives the death/grave association direct in-text support
It aligns with the dominant historical reading of Matt 12:40 as tomb typology, requiring no revision of 'heart of the earth'
decisive_sources: Jeremiah 51:34 — a kingdom explicitly described as a dragon that swallows into its belly and casts out
Jeremiah 51:44 — God forces the swallowing kingdom to give back what it swallowed
Ezekiel 32:2 — Pharaoh, a king, is explicitly 'as a whale in the seas'
Ezekiel 29:3 — Pharaoh as 'the great dragon' in his rivers
Jonah 1:17; 2:1-10 — the swallow, hold, and compelled disgorging that the Jeremiah texts mirror term for term
Revelation 17:15 — sea/waters defined as peoples and nations, grounding the scaling from fish to kingdom
unresolved_objections: The identification of 'the heart of the earth' as Jerusalem rather than the tomb, and the associated three-days count, rests partly on extrabiblical witnesses (Philo, Sibylline Oracles) and a mirrored-phrase argument that remains contestable

Jonah's own 'belly of Sheol' language shows the death/grave symbolism genuinely coexists with the kingdom reading; the entry's definition does not by itself displace the resurrection typology, it reframes its mechanism
Several scene-by-scene Passion parallels (fare/thirty pieces, reeds/crown of thorns, lots) vary in evidential strength and are pattern-dependent
The day-as-thousand-years reading of Nineveh's 'three days' journey' is speculative and deferred to another work
The specific claim that Jerusalem-riding-Rome is the swallowing kingdom of the antitype depends on downstream identifications (the harlot, the beast) not proven in this chapter
